1296.title: the daily routine (dinacharya)
1296.hook: a new cricket bat gets oiled before it's played; the Charaka Samhita says something similar about a body
1296.howItsDone: In Ayurveda's daily round, abhyanga is a self-massage with warm oil before bathing, and in some Hindu families oiling a child's hair or a baby's body is a regular household practice.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the daily routine woke the senses one by one: eyes, teeth, tongue, mouth, skin.

A new cricket bat comes home, pale and smelling of fresh wood, and the first job isn't to hit anything. It's to oil it: a thin coat, rubbed in by hand, left to soak, then another. Skip it, and the wood can dry out and crack the first time a hard ball meets it. Players who care about their bats do this without being told. The Charaka Samhita makes the same kind of point, with older objects, about the human body.
screen: `A NEW BAT, OILED FIRST.` → `DRY WOOD CRACKS.` → `THE SAME POINT, ABOUT A BODY.`

segments.voice: The practice is called abhyanga: oiling and rubbing the body, a part of the classical daily round, usually before the bath. The Charaka Samhita explains it with three everyday things from its own world. Paraphrased: a clay pot, a piece of leather, the axle of a cart. Each becomes strong and holds up to use when it's oiled. So too the body, the text says: it becomes firm, its skin smooth, and it's less easily hurt by strain. The classical texts give particular care to a few places: the head, the ears, the feet. Look at the picture it chooses. The body as a well-used thing: not a temple on a shelf, not a problem to fix, but something that does work every day, carried, pressed, walked on. Things that work hard get looked after. And it's done with the hands, no machine, no specialist. It's one of the few parts of the routine where a person touches their own body slowly, all over, with care. For some people that's harder than it sounds, and that's worth noticing, gently. In some families it's done for someone else, too: a grandmother oiling a child's hair, a parent rubbing a baby's legs. Hands passing the habit down. The text frames abhyanga as health, but the gesture carries something more: the body treated as worth tending. And a plain note: oil isn't right for every skin or every condition. Like everything in the round, it's a practice to fit to a person, not a rule to force onto one.
screen: `ABHYANGA: OIL, RUBBED IN BY HAND` · `A POT, A HIDE, AN AXLE` · `A WELL-USED THING, LOOKED AFTER` · `HANDS PASSING THE HABIT DOWN`

segments.voice: No oil needed: rub your palms together until they're warm, then press slowly from wrist to elbow, then the shoulders and the back of the neck, and the soles of the feet if that's comfortable. Move as if the body were something valuable that does a lot of work, then let the hands rest. If you pray, you can give thanks for whatever part of the body carried you today.
The daily routine. Its oiling, abhyanga, treats the body like a pot, a hide or an axle: something used every day, made strong by care.
Your line: the daily routine, dinacharya. A body that works hard is worth tending. See you tomorrow.

1297.title: the daily routine (dinacharya)
1297.hook: the gym wall says go until you can't; the classical daily round says stop at half
1297.howItsDone: Ayurvedic practitioners recommend daily exercise in measure, often described as to half of one's strength, and some Hindus also practice yoga postures or brisk walking as part of a morning routine.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the daily routine reached for the oil: abhyanga, and Charaka's pot, hide and axle, made strong with care.

No pain, no gain. The poster hangs on the wall above the squat rack, and the playlist agrees: push to failure, leave nothing in the tank. Then, some mornings, the body sends the bill: a sore back, a pulled shoulder, a week on the couch. The classical daily round has exercise in it too, right after the oil. It just draws the line in a very different place, and it tells you how to find the line without a coach.
screen: `NO PAIN, NO GAIN.` → `THE BODY SENDS THE BILL.` → `EFFORT, IN MEASURE.`

segments.voice: The Sanskrit word is vyayama, exercise. The Charaka Samhita describes it, paraphrased, as bodily effort that brings steadiness and strength, to be done in measure. Between them, the two texts list what good exercise gives: lightness, the capacity for work, a stronger digestive fire, the ability to bear hardship. Then comes the measure. For a strong person in the cooler seasons, exercise to half of one's strength: ardha shakti, half strength. For others, and in other seasons, less. Half. Not to failure. Not until you can't. How do you know where half is, with no watch and no coach? Tradition answers with signs in the body: when sweat comes to the forehead and the armpits, and the breath starts coming through the mouth, that's enough. The goal is the day, not the workout. Exercise in the daily round serves a life; it's meant to leave you more able to work and digest and bear things, not wiped out. Measure is also a kind of respect: the tradition that oils the body like an axle doesn't then grind it down. And it trusts the body's own signals. Paying attention to the breath is how you find your half, which makes exercise a kind of noticing too. None of this replaces a doctor's or a coach's advice for a particular body. It's a way of seeing effort: strong, regular, and stopped while there's still something left.
screen: `VYAYAMA: EFFORT FOR STEADINESS` · `ARDHA SHAKTI: HALF STRENGTH` · `SWEAT, AND BREATH THROUGH THE MOUTH` · `STOP WHILE SOMETHING'S LEFT`

segments.voice: Sitting tall, breathe in and slowly raise both arms in front of you, as high as is comfortable, and breathe out as you lower them, a few times. Notice the breath deepening and the shoulders warming, and stop before it becomes effort, with something left. Then rest the hands in your lap and feel the pulse and the warmth settle, or rest in prayer if you pray.
The daily routine. Its exercise, vyayama, is done in measure, to half one's strength, stopping, tradition says, when sweat comes and the breath moves to the mouth.
Your line: the daily routine, dinacharya. Half strength, with the breath as your coach. Go gently.

1298.title: the daily routine (dinacharya)
1298.hook: the chapter that cleans your teeth also tells you to greet people first
1298.howItsDone: Ayurvedic texts include sadvritta, good conduct, in the daily routine, and practitioners treat truthful, kind and timely speech as part of a healthy day alongside diet and exercise.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the daily routine put effort in measure: vyayama, to half one's strength, stopped while something's left.

Same chapter, a few verses on. The Ashtanga Hridaya has just finished with teeth, eyes, oil, exercise and the bath. A reader might expect breakfast next. Instead, the text turns to people. How to speak. Whom to help. What happiness is for. A health manual, still inside its chapter on the daily routine, starts talking about kindness, as if it were part of the same morning. In the tradition's eyes, it is.
screen: `TEETH, EYES, OIL, EXERCISE, BATH.` → `THEN THE TEXT TURNS TO PEOPLE.` → `KINDNESS IN THE SAME CHAPTER.`

segments.voice: Ayurveda has a name for this: sadvritta, good conduct. In the Ashtanga Hridaya it sits right inside the daily routine. Paraphrased: every action of every being is aimed at happiness. But happiness doesn't come without dharma, without right living. So be devoted to dharma. That's a striking move for a medical text. It doesn't separate the healthy body from the good life; it says the one depends on the other. Then the text gets practical about speech, which is where a lot of conduct happens. Paraphrased again: speak at the right time. Say what's helpful, and say it in measure. Don't contradict yourself. Make it pleasant to hear. And be the one who speaks first, with a friendly face. That last pair is easy to skip past. Greet first. Don't wait for the other person to decide whether this is going to be warm. Look at where that puts kindness: in the same list as brushing your teeth. Not a grand virtue for special occasions, but daily upkeep. It also echoes Sushruta's healthy person, whose self, senses and mind are clear and content; a day of sharp words and cold silences doesn't leave a mind like that. And it's specific. Not be nice, but right time, helpful, measured, pleasant, first. Ayurveda's daily round, it turns out, doesn't end at the skin.

segments.voice: Bring to mind someone you'll likely see soon, at home, at work, in a shop, someone you usually wait for, or barely greet. See yourself speaking first, with a warm face, not a forced one, and notice what happens in the body as you picture it. Then let the picture go and rest in the breath; if you pray, you can hold that person in your prayer for a moment.
The daily routine. In the Ashtanga Hridaya it includes sadvritta, good conduct: speak helpfully, in measure, at the right time, and be the first to greet.
Your line: the daily routine, dinacharya. Kindness, kept like any other daily care. Until tomorrow.

1299.title: the daily routine (dinacharya)
1299.hook: the streetlights come on and, in some homes, a small lamp too: the day has joints, and the routine marks them
1299.howItsDone: Some Hindus pray at the day's junctions, the practice called sandhyavandana, and in some homes a lamp is lit at dusk; Ayurvedic texts also advise keeping the twilights free of meals, sleep and study.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the daily routine reached past the skin: sadvritta, good conduct, and greeting first, with a friendly face.

Dusk, and the streetlights blink on one after another down the block. In some Hindu homes, around the same moment, someone lights a small lamp in front of the family shrine. Nobody announces it. The light outside is changing, so the light inside is changed too. Back on day one hundred eighteen, the path met these joints of the day, the hours of sandhya. On the last day of the daily round, it meets them again, along with what to do when life bends the routine.
screen: `STREETLIGHTS, AND A SMALL LAMP.` → `THE DAY HAS JOINTS.` → `WHEN LIFE BENDS THE ROUTINE.`

segments.voice: Sandhya is a joining, a twilight, the meeting point of two parts of the day. Some Hindus keep prayers at these meeting points, called sandhyavandana, honoring the junctions, at dawn and at dusk, and for some at noon too. Lamps lit at dusk come from the same attention. The Ayurvedic texts notice the joints from another side. Among its rules of good conduct, paraphrased, the Charaka Samhita advises against eating, sleeping or studying at the twilights. Whatever the reasons a reader finds there, the effect is the same: the joints of the day are kept a little apart, a little quieter. So the round, which began before sunrise, has shape all day: a waking, the senses, the oil, effort in measure, kind speech, and pauses at the turns. Now the honest part. Plenty of lives don't fit a dawn-to-dusk shape. Night shifts. A newborn. Illness. A job that starts at four. Does the routine just break? Read closely, the texts already leave room. The verse about waking addressed the healthy person. Exercise was measured to strength and season. And in the Ashtanga Hridaya, the chapter after the day is the year: how the routine changes with the seasons. A routine that changes with the year isn't a rigid one. So when life bends the schedule, keep the pieces that fit, and mark the joints you actually have: waking, a meal, the end of a shift. The routine follows the person, the way the texts follow the season.
screen: `SANDHYA: THE DAY'S JOINTS` · `KEEP THE JOINTS A LITTLE QUIET` · `PLENTY OF LIVES DON'T FIT` · `THE ROUTINE FOLLOWS THE PERSON`

segments.voice: Walk through a usual day, yours, not an ideal one, and find where one part bends into the next: waking, leaving the house, a meal, coming home, the last light switched off. Choose one of those joints and see yourself pausing there for a single breath before going on. If you pray, a prayer you already know can mark that joint.
The daily routine. Dinacharya, the day's conduct, from waking to the twilight, built to bend to the person who keeps it.
Your line: the daily routine, dinacharya. A pause at the joints your day really has. That's today, done.

1300.title: the seasons
1300.hook: the fan comes down from the top shelf and the heavy blanket goes up; Ayurveda reads the year the way it read the day
1300.howItsDone: People who follow Ayurveda adjust food, sleep and activity through ritucharya, the seasonal routine, which the Ashtanga Hridaya lays out across six seasons including the rains.

segments.voice: Yesterday closed the daily routine, dinacharya: the day's joints, the twilights, and a round that bends to the person keeping it.

The fan comes down from the top shelf. The heavy blanket goes up in its place. Soup drops off the menu at home, and something cold shows up instead. Nobody holds a meeting about it. A household just shifts, a little at a time, as the weather turns. That quiet shifting is what the next part of the classical texts is about. They've walked through the day. Now they zoom out and read the whole year the same way, as a round with its own turns.
screen: `THE FAN COMES DOWN.` → `A HOUSEHOLD SHIFTS QUIETLY.` → `THE YEAR, READ LIKE THE DAY.`

segments.voice: The Sanskrit word for a season is ritu, and the seasonal routine is ritucharya, the conduct of the season, a twin to dinacharya, the conduct of the day. In its chapter on the seasons, the Charaka Samhita makes a plain promise, paraphrased: a person who knows what suits each season, in food and in activity, grows in strength and in complexion. So the seasons aren't scenery. They're something a body lives through, and keeps step with. Then a surprise for anyone raised on four seasons. The Ashtanga Hridaya divides the year into six. Shishira, the cold late winter. Vasanta, spring. Grishma, summer. Varsha, the rains. Sharad, the clear autumn after the rains. And hemanta, the early winter. Here the rains are a season of their own, not a footnote. So the year becomes a bigger day. The eye that noticed dawn and dusk now notices the turn from heat to rain. And the seasons outside meet the qualities inside: the doshas, described through hot and cold, dry and oily, light and heavy, rise and settle with the weather, and the texts suggest meeting each season with its opposite. It's local, too. A person in a snowy city or a desert town will have a different year from the one the texts describe. The lesson that travels isn't the six names. It's the habit of asking, as the weather turns: what does this season need from me?
screen: `RITUCHARYA: THE CONDUCT OF THE SEASON` · `KNOW WHAT SUITS EACH SEASON` · `SIX SEASONS, THE RAINS AMONG THEM` · `WHAT DOES THIS SEASON NEED?`

segments.voice: Notice the air on your skin, warm or cool, damp or dry, and the light where you are. Then turn inward: does the body feel heavy or light this week, hungry or not, sleepy, restless, steady? No fixing, just a weather report from the inside; if you pray, you can give thanks for the season you're in.
The seasons. Ritu, a season, and ritucharya, the conduct that keeps step with it. In the Ashtanga Hridaya, the year turns six times.

1301.title: the seasons
1301.hook: a garden wrung out by summer, then the first rain: the texts split the year into a taking half and a giving half
1301.howItsDone: Ayurvedic practitioners describe the year in two halves, adana and visarga, and adjust diet and activity to protect strength in the taking half and rebuild it in the giving half.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the seasons: ritu, a season, ritucharya, keeping step with it, and a year that turns six times in the Ashtanga Hridaya.

By the end of a long, hot summer, a garden looks wrung out. The leaves curl. The soil cracks. Even the people tending it move slower, and wilt by afternoon. Then one evening the clouds pile up, the first rain hits the dust, and the whole place smells different. Over the next weeks, green comes back. The classical texts saw the whole year as that kind of rhythm: one half that draws strength out, one half that gives it back.
screen: `A GARDEN WRUNG OUT BY SUMMER.` → `THE FIRST RAIN ON THE DUST.` → `ONE HALF TAKES, ONE HALF GIVES.`

segments.voice: The Charaka Samhita splits the year into two halves, each with three of the six seasons. The first is adana, the taking: late winter, spring and summer, while the sun travels its northern course. Paraphrased, the text says that in this half the sun and the wind grow strong, sharp and dry, and they draw moisture and strength out of the world, and out of people too. The second half is visarga, the giving, or the releasing: the rains, autumn and early winter, while the sun travels south. Here, the text says, the moon is strong, the earth is cooled by clouds, rain and wind, and strength flows back. Not hot season and cold season, but a pulling-away and a pouring-back. The text follows that through to the body. Paraphrased: people tend to be weakest at the turn where the taking ends and the giving begins, around the end of summer and the start of the rains, and strongest at the other turn, in the cold months. That changes how a low stretch looks. If the year itself has a taking half, a tired late summer is partly weather, not character, and the giving half is a time to rebuild, not just recover. The sun's turns matter in Hindu life beyond medicine, too: festivals mark the sun's turn north, among them Makar Sankranti, and some Hindus count the northern course as an auspicious time. The texts take that same turning sky and read it in the body.

As you breathe in, let it be the giving, the breath coming back slowly, cool and full, with no forcing either one. Then let the breath go on its own; if you pray, you can offer what's been taken and receive what's given.

1302.title: the seasons
1302.hook: frost on the windshield and a bigger appetite: Charaka's chapter on the seasons has a reason for both
1302.howItsDone: People who follow Ayurveda adjust food and habits through the year as the classical texts describe; in the cold months that means substantial warm food, oil on the skin and warm clothing, and in parts of India families share sesame-and-jaggery sweets at Makar Sankranti.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the seasons: a year in two halves, adana, the taking, and visarga, the giving.

Frost on a car windshield before work. Breath you can see. And by lunch, a hunger bigger than it was in summer, as if the body quietly raised its order. A bowl of something hot tastes better than it has any right to. That's usually filed under comfort food and left there. But the Charaka Samhita, one of Ayurveda's classical texts, gives the cold months a careful reading, and the bigger appetite sits right at its center. After oil, movement and good conduct, this week has walked out to the year itself. Today, the cold.
screen: `FROST ON THE WINDSHIELD.` → `A BIGGER APPETITE.` → `TODAY, THE COLD.`

segments.voice: Charaka's chapter on the seasons names two winters: hemanta, early winter, and shishira, late winter, colder and harsher. Its observation, paraphrased: in the cold, the body's fire of digestion is held in by the cold outside, and it grows strong, strong enough for heavy, substantial food. Then a sharper line. If that strong fire isn't given proper food, the text says, it turns on the body's own tissues. So winter isn't the season for skimping. The advice is warm and generous: substantial food with some richness, warm water, oil rubbed into the skin, heavy clothes, warm rooms, the sun when it's out. Three things follow. First, it's the rule from the dosha days: like increases like, and the opposite brings it down. Cold is met with warmth, dry winter air with oil. Second, the appetite isn't a fault to fight. It's the body doing its job in the cold, and the job is to feed it well. Third, the festivals sit close by. In parts of India, at Makar Sankranti in midwinter, people share sweets of sesame and jaggery, and in Maharashtra they say, roughly, take this sweet and speak sweetly. Winter food at a winter festival, given away. None of this asks you to live in an Indian winter. It asks you to look at the season you're actually in, and answer it.
screen: `HEMANTA AND SHISHIRA, THE COLD MONTHS` · `A STRONG FIRE IN THE COLD` · `FEED IT, OR IT FEEDS ON YOU` · `SESAME AND JAGGERY AT SANKRANTI`

segments.voice: Find the warmest place in the body right now, the folded hands, the chest or the belly, and rest your attention there, feeling the out-breath warm as it leaves. If there's cold at the edges, at the feet or the back of the neck, notice it without fixing it: warmth in the middle, weather at the edges. If you pray, give thanks for the last warm meal you ate.
